title: How a studio website gets inbound leads
metaTitle: How a studio site earns inbound leads
excerpt: A studio page earns inbound when it answers a search the buyer already typed, then offers a real conversation. A gallery without sentences leaves that buyer guessing.
alt: Pale blue and orange ink swirls on a white ground, a quiet field of color beside an article about pages that have to say something clear.
caption: Color on a white ground, before the sentence is written. Photograph via Unsplash.

faqs.question: What should a studio homepage say on the first screen?
faqs.answer: Name the offer, who it is for, and how to start a conversation. Put two or three projects just under that, each with one sentence about the constraint you solved. A grid of images with no sentences asks the visitor to invent a reason to write, and most people will leave instead.

faqs.question: How many projects does an inbound page need?
faqs.answer: Enough that a skeptical founder can see the kind of problem you have already held. Two or three captioned projects beat a long grid of unlabeled crops. Retire work that no longer matches the offer, even when the pictures are the strongest thing on the site.

faqs.question: Where should the contact action sit?
faqs.answer: Put one action at the end of the answer, and repeat it for people who reach the bottom of the page still looking. Say what the conversation will decide: fit, the shape of the work, and whether a proposal is worth writing. A long form before that conversation spends interest you have already earned.

sources.title: How Long Do Users Stay on Web Pages?

markdown:
Design studio inbound leads start when a page answers a search the buyer already has, and then offers a conversation. A portfolio of images, with no sentence about the job, does not start that path.

The page has to be specific enough to quote. A founder should be able to say what you do, who it is for, and how to talk to you, without opening a deck.

## Name the search before you design the page

Buyers arrive with a job. A marketing site for a product they cannot explain. A store move that must not break checkout. A brand system a team of five will actually use. Your page should be able to sit under one of those sentences.

Write the sentence before the layout. If you cannot name the search, you are arranging pictures. The search can be narrow. Narrow is how a small studio meets the right person. A page that claims every industry you have touched becomes a page for nobody in particular.

[Google's people-first guidance](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/fundamentals/creating-helpful-content) asks whether a page has a primary purpose, and whether a reader can tell who made it. A homepage that is only a mood fails both tests. A page that says you design and build marketing sites and product interfaces for early teams has a purpose. Your name on the work answers the authorship question.

Keep one offer in the title and on the first screen. A second offer can live further down, labeled, so it does not compete with the sentence that earned the visit. Founders forward the first sentence. They rarely forward a paragraph of capabilities.

## Put sentences on the work

The first screen should carry the offer and the next step. [Nielsen Norman Group's research](https://www.nngroup.com/articles/how-long-do-users-stay-on-web-pages/) on how long people stay is blunt about that window. Visitors often leave within 10 to 20 seconds, and a clear value proposition has to land inside about 10 seconds if you want any more of their time. Spend those seconds on the offer. A slogan that could belong to any studio spends them on atmosphere.

Then show the work with a sentence on each project. The sentence names the constraint. Down the Cove is an ecommerce migration and redesign. Thomas Bewick is an editorial heritage site. Ballarat Box Sports is a community sports brand. Got Next, Leadly, and Trade Moai are product interfaces. Wabisabi is a calmer, tactile brand world. A buyer who needs a store can see a store. A buyer who needs an interface can see an interface.

Keep the stack in the background until it answers a fear. If the buyer has been left with a site they cannot edit, say that the repository is theirs, and that the public site is built in Next.js, React, and TypeScript, styled with Tailwind, and shipped on Vercel. If they have been burned by motion that ignores a request for less of it, say that motion has a reduced-motion path. Those are facts about the making. They are not a feature grid.

Captions do more inbound work than crops. A beautiful crop with no decision asks the visitor to invent the story. One line under the image, in the same voice as the homepage, is enough. The line should still make sense if the image fails to load.

## Make proof a decision, not a gallery

A short case note earns trust when it records a choice. What the page was supposed to do. What you refused. What the client kept. Three paragraphs of that kind beat a long story that never names the constraint.

Place the proof next to the offer it supports. A services block about product interfaces should show product interfaces. A services block about stores should show a store. Mixing them without a label makes the range look unfocused, even when the range is real.

You need enough projects that a skeptical founder can see the kind of problem you have already held. Leave unpublished work described in general terms. Skip invented results, invented quotes, and invented timelines. An honest constraint is stronger than a number you cannot stand behind on a call.

If a project is old and the way you work has changed, say what changed. A site from several years ago, presented as current practice, will be questioned in the first meeting. The meeting will then be about the gap. Update the sentence, or retire the image, before you send the link.

A useful case note can stay short:

- The job the page had to do for a stranger.
- The decision that shaped the structure.
- What the client can edit after launch, and what lives in code.
- The limit: what this project does not prove.

That list is easier to write than a narrative, and easier for a buyer to skim between meetings.

## End the answer with a conversation

Inbound dies in the last inch when the page answers the question and then offers a row of social icons. The next step should match the page. A founder who just understood the offer is ready for a short call. A twelve-field qualification form spends that readiness on data entry.

Say what the call is for. Fit, the shape of the work, and whether a proposal is worth writing. Say what the call will not do. It will not design the site in half an hour. That limit is part of the offer. It tells a serious buyer you know the size of the work.

Put the action where the answer ends. Repeat it once for the person who scrolled with a private question. One action. Two equal buttons force a choice the page should already have made.

On a Hanabi project the public site is the inbound surface. The client portal comes later, for brand files, docs, and updates once the work is underway. A stranger should be able to ask a question without an account. Keep the front door and the project room as different rooms, with different jobs.

Write the button in the buyer's language. "Book a 30-minute intro" says what they get. "Let's connect" says nothing about the length, the purpose, or who will be on it. The sentence next to the button can name what to bring: the current site, the offer in one line, and the decision you are trying to make.

## Publish in an order a buyer can follow

Start with four surfaces, in this order.

1. A homepage that names the offer, shows two or three projects with sentences, and offers a call.
2. A services page that lists the work in the buyer's language, with a boundary on each line.
3. Proof, either as its own page or woven into the first two, so the work is not an island.
4. One article that answers a question you hear on every intro call.

That article is the inbound engine. It should be useful if the reader never hires you. It should also make the next step obvious. A library of posts that never says how to start is a magazine. One post that answers a real objection is a better start than twenty thin ones.

Write it the way you would answer in a meeting. The decision first. The steps second. The limit of the advice at the end, so a homepage structure is not asked to repair a confused offer.

Name the pages the way a buyer would search and the way they would forward a link. Internal nicknames can stay in the repository. The visible heading can carry a little more of the brand than the title element. Both should still describe the job of the page. A heading called "Work" travels poorly. "Marketing sites for early product teams" can be pasted into a chat, and the recipient knows what they will open.

Give each page one job. The homepage introduces. The services page sets boundaries. The proof page shows decisions. The article answers one hard question. When a page tries to do all four, the opening window is spent on navigation rather than the offer.

## Watch whether the page earns the call

Watch the queries that bring people, and watch whether those people reach a conversation. A page can attract visits and still fail when the first paragraph disagrees with the query that brought them. Read the query. Read your opening out loud. If they describe different jobs, fix the opening before you add another section.

Ask the people who book where they came from. The first minute of the call is enough. You are listening for a pattern: which page, which sentence, which project. Do more of that pattern. Retire pages that attract work you do not want, even when the traffic chart looks healthy.

Keep the first sentence fast to arrive. A hero that plays before the offer is readable spends the opening on a loading state. Treat the offer as the content that must paint. Treat motion as something that can wait until the person has a reason to stay. When you use motion, it should show a relationship, such as a panel coming from the button that opened it, and it should have a reduced-motion version.

Review the page on a phone, on ordinary wifi, the way a buyer will. A layout that only works on a wide monitor is a layout for your own desk. Search traffic is often a phone in a hallway between meetings. If the offer wraps into a slogan and the button sits below a full-screen image, the page has hidden the two things the visit came for.

## What a page cannot do

A clear page cannot create demand for an offer nobody wants. It also cannot replace a conversation when the project is unusual, regulated, or still a sketch. Inbound is a filter. It should attract the work you can do well and let the rest pass.

If the pictures are strong and the sentences are missing, write the sentences before you redesign the grid. If the sentences are clear and the work on the page is unrelated to them, replace the proof. If both are in place and the right people are still absent, the next problem may be distribution. Distribution pointed at a vague homepage is an expensive way to learn that the page was not ready.

The pages a cold visitor needs, before any ad spend, are the subject of [what to publish before you run ads](/blog/what-to-publish-before-you-run-ads). Read that next if you are close to buying traffic and you want the site to hold the visit.

When the offer, the proof, and the next step are clear enough to say out loud, book [an intro call with Hanabi](https://cal.com/hanabi/30min). Bring the page. The half hour should tell you whether the site can receive the search you want, or whether the sentences still have to be written.
